name: Teriparatide
lead: Teriparatide is a recombinant form of the first 34 amino acids of human parathyroid hormone (PTH 1-34), the portion that activates the PTH1 receptor [1][26]. It is a prescription bone-anabolic drug given by daily subcutaneous injection to treat osteoporosis, and was first marketed by Eli Lilly as Forteo [1][2]. Unlike most osteoporosis drugs, which slow bone breakdown, it stimulates new bone formation [1].

Its approved uses are postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk, men with primary or hypogonadal osteoporosis, and men and women with glucocorticoid-associated osteoporosis [1][2][26]. Randomised trials show it reduces vertebral fractures; in the 1,637-woman registration trial new vertebral fractures occurred in 14 percent of placebo recipients versus 5 percent on the 20 microgram dose, and in a head-to-head trial it outperformed an oral bisphosphonate on new vertebral fractures in women with severe osteoporosis [29][11][2].

Its connection to appearance is mostly through the skeleton's role in stature and posture: by lowering the rate of new vertebral fractures, bone-building treatment is aimed at preserving the spine's shape, which clinicians associate with keeping height and avoiding a stooped posture. Teriparatide also appears in some looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forum discussion as one of several substances speculated to promote bone formation. No published study has tested it for cosmetic skeletal or facial-bone change in healthy adults, and its regulatory approvals cover osteoporosis only.

paras: The US label lists treatment of postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high risk of fracture (a prior osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors, or failure of or intolerance to other therapy), increasing bone mass in men with primary or hypogonadal osteoporosis at high risk, and osteoporosis associated with sustained systemic glucocorticoid therapy [26][1]. Clinical overviews position anabolic agents such as teriparatide, abaloparatide and romosozumab for people at especially high near-term fracture risk, such as those with very low bone density or previous vertebral or hip fractures [4][13].

Treatment has typically been limited to a lifetime maximum of about two years, after which an antiresorptive drug is generally recommended to preserve gains in bone density [2]. Off-label use has been explored in other skeletal conditions, including osteogenesis imperfecta, and in fracture healing, for which small registered trials exist [2][24].

There is no approved cosmetic use. Forum members have raised the idea that bone-forming substances might thicken or enlarge bones, mostly in discussion of bone size for physique or frame, and the idea appears in a few looksmaxxing-adjacent threads [28]. No published research has examined teriparatide for jaw, facial or other cosmetic bone change in healthy adults.
The label advises avoiding teriparatide in people with open growth plates (epiphyses), which places growing adolescents outside its approved use [26].

Where research touches the jaw and mouth, it concerns disease rather than shape. A 2018 review of anabolic agents beyond osteoporosis reported a randomised placebo-controlled trial in severe chronic periodontitis with better clinical outcomes, greater resolution of alveolar bone defects and faster wound healing with teriparatide, and described case reports and small studies in osteonecrosis of the jaw while concluding the evidence was too limited to recommend it for that condition [31].

The pivotal Fracture Prevention Trial randomised 1,637 postmenopausal women with prior vertebral fractures to daily parathyroid hormone (1-34) at 20 or 40 micrograms or to placebo, with a median observation of about 21 months. New vertebral fractures occurred in 14 percent of the placebo group and 5 percent and 4 percent of the two treatment groups, and nonvertebral fragility fractures in 6 percent versus 3 percent. Both doses increased lumbar spine and femoral neck bone density, and the authors reported the side effects as minor, mainly occasional nausea and headache [29]. Grokipedia summarises the result as roughly 65 percent fewer vertebral and 53 percent fewer nonvertebral fragility fractures [2], and Wikipedia describes about an 8 percent spinal bone-density increase after one year and a reduced hip-fracture risk, with no reduction in forearm or wrist fracture [1].

The VERO trial enrolled 1,360 postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis and compared daily teriparatide with weekly risedronate over 24 months. New radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in 5.4 percent of the teriparatide group and 12.0 percent of the risedronate group (risk ratio 0.44), and clinical fractures in 4.8 percent versus 9.8 percent; nonvertebral fragility fractures differed by less (4.0 versus 6.1 percent) and the gap was not statistically significant. The study was funded by Lilly [11].

A living systematic review and network meta-analysis for the American College of Physicians (34 randomised trials plus 36 observational studies) reported that abaloparatide and teriparatide reduced clinical and vertebral fractures but were associated with more withdrawals due to adverse events, and noted that few studies included men or treatment beyond three years [3]. In glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, a trial compared teriparatide with alendronate [16].

The DATA trial found that combining teriparatide with denosumab increased bone mineral density more than either drug alone, and its switch extension examined transitions between the two agents [8][7]. Wikipedia notes that switching from denosumab to teriparatide has been associated with progressive or transient bone loss [1]. Reviews also compare teriparatide with abaloparatide, a PTHrP analogue, and with romosozumab [4][5][6][10].
Clinical research on teriparatide is extensive but concerns osteoporosis, fracture healing and related bone disease, not appearance.

Randomised trials include the 2001 Fracture Prevention Trial against placebo [29], the VERO trial against risedronate in severe osteoporosis [11], the DATA and DATA-Switch trials combining or sequencing teriparatide with denosumab [8][7], a comparison with alendronate in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis [16], and a phase 2 study of an oral PTH(1-34) tablet in postmenopausal women [9]. A related PTHrP analogue, abaloparatide, was tested against placebo for vertebral fractures in the ACTIVE trial [6], and romosozumab was tested in a phase 2 trial in postmenopausal women with low bone density [10].

Registered trials include comparisons of biosimilar or reformulated teriparatide products with Forteo in patients and healthy volunteers, a microneedle-patch PTH dose-ranging study, an imaging study of bone structure, a trial in ankle fractures, and a nasal-spray study [18][19][20][23][21][22][24][25]. Reviews describe the effects of teriparatide, abaloparatide and romosozumab in postmenopausal osteoporosis [4], and general osteoporosis overviews place anabolic therapy in clinical context [12][13][14][15].

The 2018 review Anabolic agents: what is beyond osteoporosis? summarises off-label uses. In spine fusion, animal studies generally showed higher fusion rates, human studies reported higher or earlier fusion, and one randomised trial in women found fusion in 69.0 percent with teriparatide versus 35.1 percent without treatment; the authors called this the best-supported off-label area [31].

For fracture healing, a randomised trial of 102 women with distal radius fractures found a shorter median healing time (7.4 versus 9.1 weeks) on the 20 microgram dose but not the 40 microgram dose, and a prospective study in elderly pelvic fracture patients reported 7.8 versus 12.6 weeks; evidence for non-unions and stress fractures is limited to case reports and small studies, and the authors describe the roles in arthroplasty, jaw osteonecrosis and fragility-fracture healing as controversial [31]. Registered trials include one in ankle fractures [24].

Common reactions listed on the US label include arthralgia, pain and nausea; other effects reported in clinical use include headache, dizziness, leg cramps, orthostatic hypotension and raised blood calcium [26][1][2]. The label also describes hypersensitivity reactions, hypercalcaemia and skin calcification, urolithiasis and a risk of digoxin toxicity [26].

Osteosarcoma developed in rats given high doses for much of their lifetime, which led to a boxed warning and limits on treatment duration; human surveillance has not demonstrated an increased risk, and the FDA removed the boxed warning in November 2020 [1][2]. The label still advises avoiding use in people at increased baseline risk of osteosarcoma, such as those with Paget's disease of bone, prior skeletal radiation therapy, open growth plates, bone metastases or a history of skeletal malignancy [26][1]. There are no adequate data in pregnant women, and the label recommends considering discontinuation when pregnancy is recognised [26].

The osteosarcoma question has its own history. The registration trial was stopped early, after a median of about 19 months, when a long-term rat study showed dose-dependent osteosarcoma at high doses; a second rat study at a clinically relevant dose found no bone tumours over 20 months, and a monkey study found none, and an expert board judged the rat findings unlikely to predict human risk. The FDA approved Forteo in 2002 with a boxed warning, a recommended two-year lifetime limit, a risk-mitigation programme and a postmarketing surveillance requirement [30].

Surveillance published in a JBMR Plus review included an osteosarcoma study that observed 3 cases against about 4.17 expected (standardised incidence ratio 0.72), a registry linking 75,247 patients to 6,180 osteosarcoma cases with no matches, a Medicare linkage with no osteosarcoma among 153,316 users, and a commercial claims study with 3 cases among 379,283 users; across about 2.47 million treated patients the authors reported incidence did not exceed background rates. The boxed warning was removed effective 16 November 2020, the osteosarcoma warning text was retained, and the lifetime two-year limit was revised so that longer use can be considered in people who remain at high fracture risk [30]. Wikipedia describes the risk as extremely rare, about 1 in 100,000 [1].

Endogenous 84-amino-acid PTH is the primary regulator of calcium and phosphate metabolism in bone and kidney, and teriparatide and the 34 N-terminal residues bind the same receptors with the same affinity [26]. Sustained high PTH increases bone resorption and depletes bone, whereas intermittent exposure, as with once-daily injection, activates osteoblasts more than osteoclasts and so produces net bone formation [1]. Laboratory work on osteoclast-like cell formation and its regulation by hormones underlies understanding of how PTH acts in bone [17]. The effect is largest in trabecular (spongy) bone such as the vertebrae [2].

Teriparatide is identical in sequence to the first 34 amino acids of human PTH and is produced by recombinant DNA technology [1][26]. Abaloparatide is a related analogue of PTH-related peptide with a different binding profile at the receptor [5].

Teriparatide is the amino-terminal 34-residue fragment of parathyroid hormone, the part that carries its receptor-binding activity [1][26]. Interest in PTH as a bone builder rather than a bone dissolver rests on the observation that intermittent exposure favours formation while continuous exposure favours resorption [1]. Eli Lilly and Company carried out the formal clinical development of the fragment, leading to the large registration trial reported in 2001 [29][30].

Teriparatide was approved for medical use in the United States in 1987, according to Wikipedia, and the FDA approved Forteo for osteoporosis in men and postmenopausal women at high fracture risk on 26 November 2002; EU authorisation followed in June 2003 [1][2]. A recombinant product (Bonsity, from Pfenex and marketed by Alvogen) was approved in the United States in October 2019 through the 505(b)(2) pathway and launched in June 2020; Canada approved Osnuvo in January 2020; and European biosimilars followed, with Qutavina and Livogiva authorised in August 2020, Sondelbay in March 2022 and Kauliv in February 2023 [1]. The FDA removed the osteosarcoma boxed warning in November 2020 [30].

Teriparatide is available only by prescription in the United States, the European Union, Canada (Schedule D) and Australia (Schedule 4) [1]. Brand and biosimilar names include Forteo, Forsteo, Bonsity, Qutavina, Livogiva, Osnuvo, Sondelbay and Kauliv [1]. The label's use limits and contraindications (open growth plates, Paget's disease of bone, prior skeletal radiation, bone metastases or skeletal malignancy) apply to the approved indications [26].

Community mentions are sparse. A 2013 T Nation thread on bone size lists teriparatide, with growth hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin, among substances said to contribute to bone formation, in the context of whether bones can be thickened [28]. Another thread notes the Wikipedia teriparatide page in a discussion of bone health in low testosterone [27]. Within these discussions the drug is generally raised as a treatment for bone loss rather than as an established cosmetic tool.

timeline.event: Teriparatide approved for medical use in the United States, according to Wikipedia [1].
Fracture Prevention Trial (1,637 women) reports fewer vertebral and nonvertebral fractures versus placebo; the trial had been stopped early after rat osteosarcoma findings [29][30].
FDA approves Forteo (Eli Lilly) for osteoporosis in men and postmenopausal women at high fracture risk, with a boxed warning and two-year limit [1][2][30].
Authorised in the European Union as Forsteo; osteosarcoma surveillance study begins in the United States [1][30].
Trial comparing teriparatide with alendronate in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis published [16].
DATA trial reports combined teriparatide and denosumab in postmenopausal women [8].
VERO trial reports fewer new vertebral fractures than risedronate [11].
FDA approves recombinant teriparatide product Bonsity; first generic versions approved [1][2].
FDA removes the boxed osteosarcoma warning (November) and revises the two-year lifetime limit; Osnuvo approved in Canada; EU approves Qutavina and Livogiva [1][30].
Network meta-analysis for the American College of Physicians evaluates fracture-prevention treatments including teriparatide [3].

lore.intro: Teriparatide is mentioned only occasionally on forums, usually as a bone-health drug in testosterone and hormone threads and, in a few posts, as a substance said to contribute to bone formation [28][27].

claims.claim: Bone-forming drugs like teriparatide can thicken bones
claims.believers: A poster in a 2013 T Nation thread on bone size lists teriparatide alongside growth hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin as substances that contribute to bone formation, and asks how much and which bones could thicken [28].
claims.experts: Teriparatide is approved to increase bone mass and reduce fractures in people with osteoporosis, with its largest effects in trabecular bone [26][2]. No published study has tested it for enlarging bones or changing facial structure in healthy adults.

claims.believers: A forum post linking the Wikipedia article states that it does not seem to have side effects [27].
claims.experts: The US label lists arthralgia, pain and nausea as common reactions and describes hypercalcaemia, urolithiasis, hypotension and hypersensitivity; the osteosarcoma boxed warning, based on rat studies, was removed in 2020 after human surveillance did not show increased risk [26][2].

claims.claim: Teriparatide is used for low-testosterone bone loss.
claims.believers: A user in a low-testosterone thread links the Wikipedia page when discussing bone health [27].
claims.experts: The US label covers increasing bone mass in men with primary or hypogonadal osteoporosis at high fracture risk [26].

claims.claim: Because it is a bone-forming drug, it could be used to enlarge or thicken facial bones.
claims.believers: Posters in a bone-size thread list teriparatide among substances that contribute to bone formation and ask which bones could thicken [28].
claims.experts: The label advises avoiding use with open growth plates, research on the jaw concerns periodontal defects and osteonecrosis, and no published study has tested it for facial-bone change in healthy adults [26][31].

angle.text: Teriparatide is a medical bone-builder; its documented payoff is stronger bone and fewer vertebral fractures in people with osteoporosis. Forum users speculate about bone thickness and frame, a use that has not been studied in healthy adults [26][28].
